extracted.intended_audience: general readers, students and researchers interested in humor, ethnic stereotypes, and cultural history
extracted.subtask_description: Describing and contextualizing the English-language phenomenon known as the 'Polish joke' — an ethnic joke targeting Polish people — including its definition, examples, historical origins, stereotypical content, and social impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Type of joke — ethnic joke
rubrics_metrics.description: Polish joke is an English-language ethnic joke deriding Polish people, based on derogatory stereotypes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classifies the genre: this is an ethnic joke (targeting an ethnic group) rather than a non-ethnic comedic form. The infobox explicitly lists 'Type of joke: Ethnic joke.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Target of joke — Polish people
rubrics_metrics.description: The target of the Polish joke is Polish people.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Infobox and opening lines identify Polish people as the object of derision; the article discusses how media portrayals and historical prejudice have shaped jokes aimed at Poles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Language — English-language phenomenon
rubrics_metrics.description: Polish joke is described as an English-language ethnic joke (though comparable jokes exist in other languages/cultures).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article frames the phenomenon primarily in the context of English-language usage and American/German examples, noting how versions were brought to the United States and appeared in German popular culture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conditional-joke structure (requires prior knowledge)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Polish joke belongs in the category of conditional jokes, whose full understanding requires the audience to have prior knowledge of what a Polish joke is.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a structural/comprehension criterion: such jokes rely on shared cultural knowledge or expectations for their punchlines to land; the article explicitly names this category.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dependence on listener's preconceived notions and antipathies
rubrics_metrics.description: As with all discriminatory jokes, Polish jokes depend on the listener's preconceived notions and antipathies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluative point about how the humor functions: comprehension and offensiveness hinge on audience-held stereotypes and prejudices; this is given as a general explanatory principle in the opening.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of offensive terms/slurs (e.g., 'Polack')
rubrics_metrics.description: Sometimes an offensive term for a Pole, such as 'Polack', is used in the joke.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Flag for producers/evaluators: these jokes may include explicit slurs; the article gives this as an example of how offensiveness is manifest in language choice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stereotypical content — portrayal of inferior intelligence or backwardness
rubrics_metrics.description: Polish jokes often rely on negative stereotypes portraying Poles as 'backward' or of inferior intelligence; Hollywood and TV portrayals contributed to this perception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article cites the book 'Hollywood's War with Poland' and TV shows to show how media conditioned audiences to see Polish people as having inferior intelligence — a recurring stereotype used in jokes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stereotypical content — attribution of criminality/economic misconduct
rubrics_metrics.description: Some jokes attribute criminal behavior or economic misconduct to Poles (e.g., jokes about automobile theft or the Polish economy).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: German examples given (tourism slogan: 'Come to Poland – your car's already here') illustrate jokes that cast Poles as thieves; this is a common thematic variant to watch for when analyzing such jokes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical and propagandistic origins/context
rubrics_metrics.description: Origins and persistence of Polish jokes are linked to historical discrimination and propaganda (e.g., German anti-Polish sentiment, Nazi propaganda, 19th/20th-century regional hostilities, migration patterns).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contextual criterion for analysis: understanding a joke's content and spread requires attention to historical forces (Partitions of Poland, German Eastern Marches Society, Nazi propaganda, Cold War-era media). The article discusses competing theories of origin (e.g., 'purely American phenomenon' vs. influence of Nazi/Soviet propaganda).

rubrics_metrics.name: Social impact and public reaction (complaints, activism)
rubrics_metrics.description: Polish jokes have provoked protests and activism (e.g., Polish American organizations made efforts to challenge stereotyping; notable complaints against public figures).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating or producing such material, consider documented social responses: diplomatic complaints, organizational anti-bigotry efforts, and public outrage are part of the metric for social harm and acceptability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Example format — lightbulb/one-liner structure
rubrics_metrics.description: The article gives a classic example (lightbulb joke): 'How many Polacks does it take to change a light bulb? Three – one to hold the bulb, and two to turn the ladder.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrates a common joke structure (one-liner/lightbulb joke) employed to convey the stereotype; useful as an example of form when analyzing humor mechanics and punchline delivery.
